svg.aria-label: Diagram: Terraform on Azure, contrasting ARM and Bicep which hold no state because Resource Manager is the record, with Terraform which keeps its own state file and therefore compares three things — configuration, state and Azure — the four jobs state does, the azurerm backend with blob lease locking and encryption at rest, the authentication ladder from access key to Microsoft Entra ID, and the drift failure where a change made outside Terraform can make it plan a delete and recreate
svg.title: Terraform keeps its own record of what exists, and every difference from ARM and Bicep follows from that one fact
svg.text: ARM and Bicep have no state because Resource Manager is the state.
Terraform keeps its own record, so it compares three things instead of two — and the third one can disagree with the other two.
ARM and Bicep — two things
the template you submit
what Azure currently holds
Resource Manager reconciles the two on every
deployment. There is nothing to keep, nothing to
lock, and nothing to lose.
Terraform — three things
the configuration you wrote
the state file it maintains
what Azure currently holds
Drift is the gap between the second and the third.
It is a concept the other two cannot have.
Four jobs the state file does, and why none of them are optional
Mapping
which real Azure resource a block in your configuration refers to
Dependency metadata
the order to destroy in, needed precisely when the configuration is gone
Attribute cache
so a plan does not have to read every resource back from the API
Team synchronisation
one shared snapshot, with locking, instead of one per laptop
State is a necessary requirement for Terraform to function. It is not a cache you can delete and rebuild.
Where it should live
backend "azurerm" { ... }
A blob in a container. Blobs are automatically locked
before any operation that writes state, which is what
prevents two runs corrupting it.
Data is encrypted before being persisted, and state is
held in local memory rather than written to disk — so
no copy is left on a laptop.
How it should authenticate
Access key and SAS token — not recommended
for new workloads.
Microsoft Entra ID — recommended.
use_azuread_auth = true
The state blob is a data plane object, so the role is
Storage Blob Data Contributor on the container —
a control plane role reaches none of it.
The failure that comes from having two records: a change made outside Terraform
Microsoft’s own worked example is a storage account conversion. It changes properties outside Terraform, and if Terraform sees
them before the configuration is updated, it might plan to delete and recreate the account — downtime or data loss, from a plan
that looks routine.
The documented guard rails, in order: turn off automatic approval and read every plan for unexpected replacement; set
prevent_destroy = true
in the lifecycle block; ignore the converting property for the duration; then reconcile with
terraform apply -refresh-only
and confirm a clean plan before removing the guards.
And the fact that decides how state is protected: Terraform state is stored in plain text and might contain secrets.
Sources: Store Terraform state in Azure Storage on Microsoft Learn; Terraform state purpose and the azurerm backend on developer.hashicorp.com.
